strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly demonstrates the over-confidence issue in RLVR-trained models across multiple LLM families and scales (Fig. 3-4), with practical importance for high-stakes deployment

Novel theoretical insight: Elegant formalization of gradient conflict between accuracy and calibration objectives using Fisher-metric inner product (Prop. 4.2), providing principled justification for decoupling approach

Comprehensive experimental validation: Evaluation on 5 mathematical reasoning benchmarks with multiple calibration metrics (ECE, PCE, AUROC), strong baselines, and thorough ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution

Strong practical results: Achieves 71.6% relative ECE reduction while maintaining accuracy on par with GRPO (60.8% vs 60.4%), directly solving the accuracy-calibration tradeoff exhibited by coupled methods (RLCR, CCGSPG)

Clear presentation: Well-structured paper with effective visualizations (particularly Fig. 1, 2), comprehensive proofs in appendix, and detailed reproducibility information (hyperparameters, evaluation protocol)

Detailed analysis of method behavior: Provides evidence of stable optimization dynamics (Fig. 7), balanced confidence distributions (Fig. 8), and demonstrates consistent improvements across training steps (Fig. 6)
weaknesses: Limited theoretical rigor: The connection between mode collapse (Prop. 4.1) and over-confidence relies on informal arguments about distribution shift. The claim that extreme logit margins induce over-confident neighborhoods lacks formal justification. How common is such distribution shift in practice?

Independence assumption questionable: Theorem 5.1 claims π_θ(c|q,y) optimizes 'independently' of π_θ(y|q), but both originate from shared model parameters. While masking prevents direct gradient interference, subtle couplings through embeddings and attention patterns likely persist

Limited evaluation scope: (1) Single model tested (Qwen3-8B); generalization to other architectures/scales unclear despite base calibration analysis across models. (2) Restricted to mathematical reasoning; applicability to code generation, QA, other domains unknown. (3) Computational overhead of verbalized confidence not analyzed

Insufficient hyperparameter analysis: λ set to 0.5 with no sensitivity analysis. DCPO-G achieves better ECE (0.038 vs 0.049) but lower accuracy—suggesting DCPO may be suboptimal. No analysis of group size G or confidence targets. Missing statistical significance testing and error bars

Incomplete theoretical coverage: Proposition 4.2 assumes over-confidence and Cov(R,ϕ)>0, limiting applicability. Gradient conflict only proven for over-confident regime. Early training dynamics when assumptions may not hold unexplored

Incremental methodological contribution: Individual components (verbalized confidence, decoupling, group-level aggregation) are established techniques. Solution is relatively straightforward application of known strategies rather than novel algorithmic innovation

Missing experimental rigor: (1) No reported error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds. (2) All results from step 120 checkpoint only—potential selection bias. (3) No failure case analysis or discussion of when DCPO underperforms

strengths: Novel identification and formalization of gradient conflict between accuracy and calibration optimization using Fisher-metric analysis, providing valuable theoretical insight into why coupled optimization fails

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 mathematical and 3 code generation benchmarks with multiple metrics (accuracy, ECE, PCE, AUROC) and strong baselines, demonstrating consistent improvements
Solid theoretical foundation with four main findings (mode collapse, gradient conflict, low-variance group supervision, statistical optimality) supported by rigorous proofs in appendices
Practical method that integrates seamlessly into existing RLVR pipelines without requiring external annotations, achieving 71.6% relative ECE reduction while maintaining accuracy parity with GRPO
Thorough supplementary analysis including gradient norm dynamics, confidence distributions, ablation studies, and sensitivity analyses that provide strong insights into method behavior
Clear presentation with well-structured paper, informative figures, and detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Core contribution of decoupling objectives is standard in multi-objective optimization; limited conceptual novelty beyond applying this established principle to the RLVR calibration problem

Theoretical analysis has gaps: Proposition 4.2 assumes conditions (positive correlation, over-confidence) validated empirically but not proven universal; mode collapse analysis doesn't account for entropy regularization commonly used in practice

Hybrid calibration objective (Eq. 21) mixing instance and group-level accuracy lacks theoretical justification; Fisher-metric analysis may not apply to standard SGD without explicit natural gradient steps
Limited experimental scope: main results on 8B models only (14B in appendix); evaluation restricted to math and code domains; group size (G=8) sensitivity not analyzed; only 3 training epochs
Structured output requirement constrains applicability; while format violations decrease quickly, computational overhead of verbalized confidence generation not comprehensively analyzed
Method specifics not fully justified: λ=0.5 choice appears somewhat arbitrary; structural penalty value (-1.0) lacks justification; specific calibration loss design rationale unclear

Incomplete experimental comparisons: RLCR/CCGSPG only compared on AIME24; ConfClass baseline relatively weak; no comparison with stronger post-hoc calibration methods or evaluation on downstream tasks where calibration matters
Missing analysis of failure modes, when calibration improvements matter for user decisions, and inference-time computational costs compared to baselines

strengths: Clear problem identification: Comprehensive empirical evidence (Figures 3-5) demonstrating that RLVR exacerbates over-confidence, a genuine practical concern for LLM deployment

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple benchmarks (5 math reasoning, 3 code generation), multiple calibration metrics (ECE, PCE, AUROC), and consistent improvements across domains (71.6% relative ECE reduction)
Systematic component validation: Thorough ablation studies (Table 3) validating each design component, with results across different model families and scales (appendix)
Practical pragmatic design: DCPO operates at multiple levels (output structure, reward design, gradient masking) with clear engineering that works in practice
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Proposition 4.1 is a standard linear programming result; Proposition 4.2's proof assumes unverified assumptions and doesn't rigorously justify why decoupling specifically solves the identified gradient conflict; Theorem 5.1 is standard statistical theory without DCPO-specific insights

Confounding experimental variables: DCPO uses verbalized confidence while baselines use token-based confidence, conflating method contribution with confidence type choice. Table 1 shows GRPO logits (90.4%) outperforms GRPO verbal (88.0%), indicating confidence type significantly impacts performance

Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing across runs. Point estimates only make it impossible to assess result reliability. Hyperparameter tuning fairness unclear—was DCPO's λ tuned more carefully than baselines' hyperparameters?

Design justifications are post-hoc: Hybrid calibration target (Eq. 21), masked gradient strategy, and verbalized confidence choice all lack principled theoretical justification beyond intuition. Why these specific designs over alternatives?

Evaluation metric limitations: ECE is sensitive to unspecified binning schemes; PCE definition (confidence > accuracy bins only) has high variance; Brier Score absent from main results despite being a standard metric. No verification that high AUROC values (0.861-0.951) indicate true calibration vs. mere discriminativeness

Generalization questions unresolved: Only tested on math reasoning + code generation; primarily Qwen3-8B; only works with GRPO; no comparison with simpler baselines (entropy regularization, temperature scaling). No ablation directly comparing confidence estimation methods on equal footing

Presentation gaps: Figure 1 is purely illustrative with no quantitative conflict analysis; code link incomplete; inconsistent notation; format enforcement mechanism underspecified; related work on uncertainty quantification in LLMs limited

strengths: Addresses a critical and timely problem—calibration degeneration in RLVR—with both theoretical and practical contributions
Provides sound theoretical analysis revealing gradient conflict between accuracy and calibration objectives (Proposition 4.2) with clear intuition (Figure 1)
Comprehensive empirical motivation in Section 3 systematically demonstrates over-confidence prevalence and RLVR's role in exacerbating it
DCPO is practical and simple to implement, leveraging existing GRPO infrastructure with clear architectural design (Figure 2)
Extensive experimental evaluation across 8 benchmarks with systematic ablations validating each component; achieves 71.6% relative ECE reduction while maintaining accuracy
Strong analysis of optimization dynamics showing DCPO's gradient stability (Figure 7) and learned confidence distributions (Figure 8) vs. baselines
Well-structured paper with clear presentation, comprehensive appendices, and generalization study across model families
weaknesses: Theoretical contributions are solid but somewhat incremental: Proposition 4.1 (mode collapse) is standard without regularization; Proposition 4.2 relies on critical assumptions (positive correlation in Eq. 9) and provides limited constructive guidance beyond decoupling

Key design choices lack strong justification: block-wise verbalized confidence not compared against implicit alternatives; hybrid calibration target (Eq. 21) appears ad-hoc; λ=0.5 choice somewhat arbitrary despite sensitivity analysis
Baseline comparisons raise concerns: RLCR/CCGSPG show dramatic accuracy drops (40%→32.8% on AIME24) without discussion of hyperparameter tuning; ConfClass AUROC gap (0.642 vs 0.914) unexplained

Evaluation scope limitations: primary experiments on Qwen3-8B only; restricted to mathematical reasoning and code generation; no error bars or significance testing; missing OOD generalization evaluation
Verbalized confidence requirement introduces practical constraints: requires structured output format; not applicable when explicit confidence undesired; failure modes and edge cases not discussed

Group-level supervision assumptions under-explored: relies on small groups (G=8) being representative; sensitivity to group size and composition not analyzed; doesn't address under-confident model regime
Reproducibility gaps: code link incomplete; token masking implementation details sparse; requires 8 A100 GPUs; no statistical significance testing across multiple runs
